source.title: Safety Subspaces are Not Linearly Distinct: A Fine-Tuning Case Study
source.authors: Kaustubh Ponkshe; Shaan Shah; Raghav Singhal; Praneeth Vepakomma

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text, including appendices, is present.
record.tranche_reason: It tests harmful fine-tuning effects and the specificity of candidate safety subspaces using weight projections and subspace-overlap measurements, rather than reproducing the original studies’ methods exactly.
record.gate_note: The study fine-tunes models on harmful data and measures harmfulness on AdvBench. It also tests whether projecting or comparing weight-update subspaces selectively captures safety. It does not measure per-token KL, prefilling, suffixes, or decoding changes. Its activation-space overlap findings are not rows for the listed versions, which concern token-position concentration or weight localization.
record.test_reason: The paper's main results argue that safety is not carried by a distinct low-rank weight subspace (V5). It projects fine-tuning updates onto, and away from, the top singular directions of alignment and safety deltas, and compares subspace overlap. As a side result, it reports AdvBench harmfulness after harmful fine-tuning (V1) for five models. T5 fits better than T2 because the study is built as an argument that the localization version is wrong.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors conclude that safety is entangled with general learning and that no linear weight or activation subspace isolates it. Projection defenses therefore cut harmfulness only at a comparable cost in utility. They add that high-impact directions may still be useful for safe fine-tuning if suitably constrained.
record.recipe_differences: The study examines fine-tuning updates, linear projections, and subspace overlap; it does not reproduce the original token-depth or refusal-bypass experiments.
record.method_sensitivity: Projection rank changes the amount of retained update and changes both utility and harmfulness; the paper reports that the two decline together under orthogonal projection. It also reports model-dependent variation in activation-space overlap, which is outside the tested claim versions.

fits_no_version.finding: Activations from harmful prompts (BeaverTails, ToxiGen) and benign prompts (MATH) overlap above the random baseline. Harmful–harmful overlap is not consistently higher than useful–harmful overlap (Section 6, Figures 5, 9, 22–26).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Harmful and benign prompts are not linearly separable in the activation subspaces of aligned or fine-tuned models.

fits_no_version.finding: Top-k alignment directions amplify both utility and harmfulness more than equal-energy random directions do (Table 1/4).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: High-impact weight directions reflect general parameter sensitivity rather than safety-specific content.

record.problems: The paper reports no uncertainty estimates for the relevant scores. Several relevant results appear only in figures, and some appendix tables are flattened or have headings that conflict with the section descriptions. The main text gives no exact values for the subspace-overlap results.
record.rows_left_out: Left out the many additional SVD-rank values, model-specific projection results, and layerwise figures in Sections 3–5 and Appendices C–I; they are not needed beyond the harmful-fine-tuning values and qualitative projection/overlap results retained. Also left out activation-space overlap analyses because they do not measure the listed versions.

untested.parts: The few-to-few-hundred example range: only a 4K harmful set and a 20% contaminated mix are used. Refusal rates and near-total compliance are also not measured; the outcome is a 1–5 average harmfulness score.
Non-linear localization, sparse neuron or weight sets, and activation-space refusal directions as a weight-localization claim. Only linear SVD subspaces of alignment and safety deltas are tested.
Harmfulness after useful-only MetaMathQA fine-tuning is not reported.

missing.what: Harmful fine-tuning harmfulness for Qwen-2.5 3B (1.47 to 2.16, base 2.53), Qwen-2.5 7B (1.30 to 2.12, base 1.90) and Llama-2 7B (1.74 to 3.41, base 4.27). Also the safety-tuned Llama-3.2 1B (3.41 to 3.79) and Llama-2 7B (3.54 to 3.84).
Contaminated fine-tuning (20% harmful, 80% MetaMathQA) raises harmfulness in all models, e.g. Llama-2 7B 1.74 to 3.08 and Llama-3.2 1B 2.80 to 3.60.
Parallel projection: top-k alignment directions raise harmfulness and utility alike compared with random directions (e.g. Qwen 1.5B at 0.25: harm 1.80 vs 1.66/1.65; utility 0.53 vs 0.50/0.50).
DPO safety-tuned replication and single-layer projection experiments, both reported as showing no separation.
missing.locator: Appendix H, Figures 15–17; Appendix I, Figures 18–19

record.verdict_notes: Harmfulness is a GPT-4o-mini 1–5 average with no uncertainty reported. Table 2 and Table 5 captions say 'Parallel' though the section describes orthogonal projection. MMLU and XSTest checks are figure-only (Appendix J). V1 is a side result; the harmful data (4K examples) far exceeds the claim's few-hundred range.

versions.untested_parts: The harmful fine-tuning uses a 4K unsafe BeaverTails subset, not a few to a few hundred examples; the reported outcome is average harmfulness, not refusal rate or near-total compliance.
No harmful-compliance outcome is reported for fine-tuning on ordinary or carefully chosen benign-only data. The contaminated condition mixes benign and harmful data.
No per-token KL divergence between aligned and base models is measured.
No compliant-opening prefill, adversarial suffix, or decoding-change intervention is tested.
The study tests candidate linear weight subspaces and their effects, not arbitrary sparse sets of weights or every possible parameter localization method.
The study does not test whether training data or objectives cause first-token shallowness.
The study does not train or evaluate methods intended to deepen safety across response tokens.

relationships.condition: Llama models (Llama-3.2 1B, Llama-2 7B), 4K harmful BeaverTails fine-tuning
relationships.reason: Harmfulness returns near base: Llama-3.2 1B goes 2.80 to 4.07 against base 4.13 (r2). Llama-2 7B goes 1.74 to 3.41 against base 4.27 (Table 4; no row yet).
relationships.display_finding: Harmfulness on Llama-3.2 1B went from 2.80 to 4.07, against 4.13 for the base model. On Llama-2 7B it went from 1.74 to 3.41, against a base of 4.27.

source_check.reason: Split the condition group: r2 supports near-complete recovery for Llama-3.2 1B (2.80→4.07; base 4.13). Llama-2 7B recovers only part of the alignment-to-base gap (1.74→3.41; base 4.27, Table 4), warranting limits_scope rather than the stated near-base rationale.

relationships.reason: Harmfulness rises but stays low on the 1–5 scale: Qwen 1.5B goes 1.55 to 2.09 against base 3.27 (r1). Qwen 3B (1.47 to 2.16) and Qwen 7B (1.30 to 2.12) are from the text, Table 4.
relationships.display_finding: Harmfulness rose from 1.55 to 2.09 for Qwen 1.5B (base 3.27), from 1.47 to 2.16 for Qwen 3B (base 2.53), and from 1.30 to 2.12 for Qwen 7B, whose base model scored 1.90.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.reason: Split the condition group: partial recovery supports limits_scope for Qwen 1.5B (r1; 1.55→2.09; base 3.27) and 3B (1.47→2.16; base 2.53). Qwen 7B reaches 2.12 from 1.30, exceeding its base score of 1.90 (Table 4), so low absolute scores alone do not establish incomplete removal relative to its base.

relationships.condition: Linear top-k SVD subspaces of alignment and safety weight deltas, five Llama and Qwen models, plus DPO and per-layer variants
relationships.reason: Removing top-k components cuts harmfulness no more selectively than random projections (r3). Harmful updates overlap most with useful updates, not with alignment or safety updates (r4, r5).
relationships.display_finding: Removing top-k components reduced harmfulness no more selectively than random projections, and harmful updates overlapped most with useful updates rather than with alignment or safety updates.
